candidates.text:
volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were an engineer before agents came along, you're rightfully skeptical about lines of code and number of PRs being used as a metric for any kind of productivity. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective as being an engineer on a large team of at least 50. 

volume didn't matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few PRs: for example you could make a one line config change and save the company millions of dollars.  

but before agents, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who is struggling to perform, on the other end you might have someone who was a "coding machine" archetype. a coding machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room and emerge with a stack of PRs that solve a huge number of problems. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you've ever worked at a large tech company before, you'll get what i mean. the thing about agents is that big tech co problems are now small-medium co problems as well. 

how do agents change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a coding machine. you have incredibly capable frontier models that can write code better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you're still producing the same number of PRs as before, why wouldn't you pause to wonder why you're not being more productive? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can't outship a human coding machine?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust (https://t.co/7fzYZV8LGH). if you haven't put in the work to trust your agent's output, it is very difficult to scale up your productivity. 

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before agents, this cost was very high - you needed to hire many software engineers with high 6 figure salaries to do the work. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time (https://t.co/gTBZx7pl14) factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 moths to a year. a single engineer with agents can do the work of tens if not hundreds of engineers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don't think has hit yet is that job of the software engineer has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce software any longer (well tbh it was never only about the code, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the software. this idea of a software factory, or a Michelin kitchen as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it's the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what's possible when you put a lot of rigor into using agents at scale

candidates.text:
Your body thinks a day is 24 hours because the sun tells it so every morning. Take away the sun, and a "day" can stretch to 48 hours without you feeling a thing.

Scientists learned how far it goes in 1962, when a 23-year-old French geologist named Michel Siffre lowered himself into an Alpine cave for 63 days with no clock and no sun. When his team called down to say time was up, he argued with them. By his own count he still had a month left.

NASA funded his next one. In 1972, Siffre spent 205 days in a Texas cave, with the French Defense Ministry watching too, because they needed to schedule sleep for nuclear submarine crews. Down there his body did something nobody expected. It stretched to a 48-hour day. 36 hours awake, 12 hours asleep, and from the inside it felt completely normal.

That mechanism explains Flamini's missing 300+ days. Your brain counts days by sleep cycles, nothing else. When each cycle quietly stretches past 24 hours, the calendar and your body stop agreeing, and you have no way to feel the gap.

She stopped counting on day 65, almost exactly where Siffre's drift kicked in. When her team finally came down to get her after 500 days, she was asleep. Her first question on the surface was who's buying the beer.

The sun wins this argument on your behalf every single morning. Light hitting your eyes at dawn is the only thing pinning your internal clock to Earth's rotation, and a cave is just what happens when it stops showing up.

candidates.text:
As a subscription brand, your flows matter more than most other brands

It decides whether you’re getting 50% churn or 5%

How to build the 3 foundation flows properly:

1. Welcome series:
- Lead with founder story and clinical proof instead of begging on price with a coupon code
- Use zero-party data from onboarding questionnaires to route subscribers into targeted email tracks based on their primary goal

2. Post-purchase sequence:
- Show clear video guides on how to take the product properly so they build a consistent daily habit
- Map out the timeline of benefits so they know exactly what changes to expect over their first 60 days
- Stack customer transformation stories to eliminate buyer's remorse before the second bottle ships

3. Sunset flow:
- Enter customers after 75 days of zero opens or clicks
- Test a steep winback offer or a free full-size product threshold on their next order
- Automatically suppress anyone who doesn't engage across a 3-email sequence so your sender reputation stays clean

Today my wife and I are hiring our first coach.

It started as a fitness blog and a YouTube channel that went nowhere. Life moved us around: Korea, Michigan, a podcast, flight school. Every chapter felt like a detour. Looking back, every one was training.

The low point was a stack of unpaid bills, and a weight I couldn't bring myself to share with Carley.

We kept going anyway. Now Carley's program, Deeply Rooted, has helped 130+ moms, and she can't coach them all alone. My job is everything around her: ads, sales, ops, and a small team of AI agents doing the repetitive work so humans can coach.

None of it happened alone. Thank you to the early clients, mentors and family who kept believing.

If you're in the messy middle, keep going. Entrepreneurship is the best personal growth program there is.
